config.title: App setup & middleware chain

intro.title: App setup & middleware chain
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a basic Express.js application from scratch, focusing on how to set up a server and use middleware. You'll learn the core concept of the middleware chain, which is a sequence of functions that process HTTP requests and responses. The main technologies involved are the Express framework, Node.js, and JavaScript constructs like functions and objects. By the end, you'll understand how to initialize an Express app, add middleware functions, and control the flow of request handling in a structured way.
intro.usecase: Middleware chains are the backbone of modern web applications, handling everything from authentication to logging in production systems. When you log into an e-commerce site, middleware validates your credentials before allowing access to your order dashboard. Payment processing platforms use middleware to sanitize input data, check for fraud patterns, and log transactions before completing purchases. API gateways rely on middleware chains to rate-limit requests, parse JSON bodies, and add CORS headers for secure cross-origin communication.

objectives: Initialize an Express application instance with the required imports
Configure basic middleware to parse incoming JSON request bodies
Construct a custom middleware function that logs request details
Integrate multiple middleware functions into the application's request-response cycle
Manipulate the middleware chain order to control execution flow
Apply error-handling middleware to catch and respond to exceptions
Bind route-specific middleware to individual endpoints

steps.title: Import Express framework
steps.instruction: Import the Express module using require()
steps.hint: Use the require() function to import the Express module and assign it to a variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: importing a module
const fs = require('fs');
steps.expectedOutcome: The Express module is imported and ready to be used to create a web server.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the Express module.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using require('express') to import the Express module.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Express module wasn't imported correctly. Use require('express') to import it.

steps.title: Create Express application instance
steps.instruction: Create an Express application instance by calling express() and assign it to a constant named 'app'.
steps.hint: Use the imported express function to create your application instance.
steps.analogousExample:
// Creating an application instance
const app = express();

successCriteria: An Express application instance is created and assigned to a constant named 'app'.

steps.title: Define a simple GET route handler
steps.instruction: Add a GET route handler for the root path ('/') that sends a response with the text 'Hello from Express!'
steps.hint: Use app.get() with '/' as the path and a callback function that takes request and response parameters. Call res.send() inside the callback.
steps.expectedOutcome: The app will respond to GET requests to the root URL with a text message.
successCriteria: A GET route handler for '/' is defined using app.get() and sends a response with 'Hello from Express!'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using app.get() with '/' as the path and sending the exact text 'Hello from Express!' in the response.
steps.feedbackWrong: add a GET route handler for the root path that sends a text response.

steps.title: Add a simple logging middleware function
steps.instruction: Define a middleware function named 'logRequest' that logs the request method and URL,
steps.hint: Middleware functions in Express take three parameters: req, res, and next. Use console.log() to output the method and URL from the request object.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a middleware function that logs each incoming request's HTTP method and URL to the console.
successCriteria: A function named 'logRequest' is defined with parameters (req, res, next), logs the request method and URL using console.log(), and calls next().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function logs both the method and URL from the request object and calls next() to continue the middleware chain.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't meet all requirements. It should be named 'logRequest', log the request method and URL, and call next().

steps.instruction: calls next() to pass control to the next middleware or route handler.
steps.hint: Middleware functions in Express take three parameters: req, res, and next. Use console.log() to output the method and URL from the request object.
steps.feedbackPartial: Review the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Register the logging middleware globally
steps.instruction: Use app.use() to register your logging middleware function so it runs for all incoming requests.
steps.hint: Call app.use() with your middleware function as the argument. Place this before your route definitions.
steps.expectedOutcome: The logging middleware will now execute for every request before reaching route handlers.
successCriteria: app.use() is called with your middleware function as argument, placed before route definitions.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling app.use() with your middleware function as the argument.
steps.feedbackWrong: The middleware isn't registered yet. Use app.use() with your middleware function to apply it to all requests.

steps.title: Add a second middleware that modifies request
steps.instruction: Define a middleware function named addTimestamp that adds a timestamp to the request object as req.requestTime and calls next().
steps.hint: Create a function that takes req, res, and next as parameters. Inside, set req.requestTime = Date.now() or new Date().toISOString(), then call next().
steps.expectedOutcome: A middleware function named addTimestamp is defined that adds a timestamp property to the request object.
successCriteria: The addTimestamp function is defined, sets req.requestTime, and calls next().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a middleware function, but check that it correctly adds req.requestTime and calls next(). Make sure it has all three parameters (req, res, next).
steps.feedbackWrong: The middleware function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function named addTimestamp that takes req, res, next parameters, sets req.requestTime, and calls next().

steps.title: Register the timestamp middleware
steps.instruction: Register your addTimestamp middleware globally using app.use(), placing it after the logging middleware in the chain.
steps.hint: Use app.use() with the middleware function name, and make sure it's placed after the existing app.use() call for logging.
steps.expectedOutcome: The addTimestamp middleware will be registered globally and will execute after the logging middleware for all incoming requests.
successCriteria: The addTimestamp middleware is registered with app.use() and placed after the logging middleware registration.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using app.use() to register the addTimestamp middleware, and that it's placed after the logging middleware registration.
steps.feedbackWrong: The timestamp middleware isn't registered correctly. Use app.use() to register the addTimestamp middleware function, placing it after the existing app.use() call for logging.

steps.title: Update route handler to use middleware data
steps.instruction: Modify your existing GET route handler to use the requestTime property added by the timestamp middleware in its response.
steps.hint: The timestamp middleware added requestTime to the request object. Access it as req.requestTime in your route handler.
steps.expectedOutcome: The GET route handler now includes the requestTime value from the middleware in its response.
successCriteria: The route handler uses req.requestTime in its response.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using req.requestTime in your route handler's response.
steps.feedbackWrong: The route handler doesn't appear to use the requestTime property from the middleware.

steps.title: Add error-handling middleware
steps.instruction: Define an error-handling middleware function named 'errorHandler' with the signature (err, req, res, next). Inside the function, set the response status to 500 and send a JSON response with an error property containing the error message.
steps.hint: Error-handling middleware in Express has four parameters instead of three. The first parameter is the error object.
steps.expectedOutcome: An error-handling middleware function named 'errorHandler' is defined with four parameters and sends a 500 status with JSON error response.
successCriteria: The errorHandler function is defined with (err, req, res, next) parameters and sends res.status(500).json({ error: err.message })
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function has exactly four parameters (err, req, res, next) and sends a JSON response with status 500.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error-handling middleware isn't defined correctly. Remember it needs four parameters and should send a JSON error response.

steps.title: Start the server and listen on a port
steps.instruction: Call app.listen() to start the Express server on port 3000.
steps.hint: Use app.listen(port, callback) where the callback logs a message to confirm the server is running.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Express server will start and listen for incoming HTTP requests on port 3000.
successCriteria: app.listen() is called with port 3000 and a callback that logs a confirmation message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling app.listen() with both the port number and a callback function that logs a message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server isn't starting correctly. You need to call app.listen() with port 3000 and provide a callback function.
